proposals.hypothesis: Li3NbO4 is a Li-rich, wide-gap niobate. Nb5+ coatings such as LiNbO3 are established for suppressing cathode-electrolyte interface reactions, and Nb5+ is not a cation the earlier La/Zr-containing contact products depended on. A Li-rich composition should keep it oxidatively stable against LiCoO2 at 4 V.

Every tested family (phosphate, fluoride, Zr/Al oxide, silicate) either reacted with LLZO to form La-containing products and O2, or had a large self-decomposition penalty. Niobate chemistry has not been tested yet.

proposal.hypothesis: Li3PO4 is a wide-gap, electronically insulating oxide-phosphate with high oxidative stability, so it should resist decomposition at the LiCoO2 interface near 4 V. It is also chemically compatible with the Li-rich LLZO garnet, and phosphate coatings are a well-established buffer layer for sulfide and oxide solid electrolytes. This makes it a strong first candidate for a low interfacial penalty.

LiF is a wide-gap, electronically insulating fluoride with very high oxidative stability, so it should resist decomposition at the LiCoO2 interface at 4 V. It is also Li-rich and thermodynamically compatible with the garnet LLZO, and fluoride coatings are commonly used on cathodes. The Li3PO4 result showed a penalty of about 0.099 eV, above the 0.05 eV target, from reaction with the LLZO contact. A fluoride with a different anion chemistry may give a lower interfacial penalty.
proposal.motivation: Li3PO4 (mp-aaaaauhx) was insulating with a wide gap but had a contact penalty of 0.099 eV/non-Li atom (bin 4, not acceptable), so I am trying a chemically distinct, Li-rich fluoride family.

proposal.hypothesis: Li2ZrO3 is a wide-gap, electronically insulating lithium oxide with high oxidative stability at 4 V, so it should resist decomposition against LiCoO2. Its Zr cation is already present in the LLZO garnet, which should reduce driving force for cation exchange and for the La/Zr-oxide and O2-releasing contact reactions that gave penalties of 0.099 and 0.12 eV for LiF and Li3PO4. Lithium zirconate is also a known cathode-coating material, so it is a chemically distinct oxide-family test after the phosphate and fluoride results.
proposal.motivation: Both prior coatings (Li3PO4 at 0.120 eV and LiF at 0.099 eV, both bin 4 or higher) reacted with LLZO to form La/Zr-containing products and O2, and neither met the 0.05 eV target. A Zr-containing Li-rich oxide should share the garnet's Zr chemistry and may avoid that reaction.

proposal.hypothesis: LiAlO2 is a wide-gap, electronically insulating lithium aluminate with high oxidative stability at 4 V against LiCoO2. Al3+ is already present in many garnet-type electrolytes, and LiAlO2 is a widely used Li-ion cathode coating. Its Al-O framework may avoid the La/Zr-oxide and O2-releasing contact reactions seen for Li3PO4, LiF and Li2ZrO3 against LLZO, which all gave penalties above 0.05 eV.

proposal.hypothesis: Li4SiO4 is a Li-rich, wide-gap oxide. Its SiO4 tetrahedral framework is thermodynamically stable and oxidatively robust at 4 V against LiCoO2. Silicates are a chemically distinct family from the phosphate, fluoride and Zr/Al oxide coatings tried so far. Its Si4+ cation is less likely than Zr4+ or Al3+ to drive the La-containing and O2-releasing reactions with LLZO that gave penalties of 0.08 to 0.30 eV/non-Li atom before.

Li2ZrO3 gave the lowest contact penalty at 0.099 eV, and LiAlO2 had a low self-decomposition penalty but a 0.12 eV contact penalty.
